notable_claims: Library principles can be applied to the selection and filtering of digital content on newsgroups, FTP archives, and Free-Nets.
classification.summary: This item is a paraphrase of a talk given at the 'Computers, Freedom, and Privacy '94' conference. The presentation advocates for applying library science principles to digital content management, including newsgroups, FTP archives, and Free-Nets. It addresses issues of censorship, filtering, and privacy in early public access systems.
classification.title: Applying library principles to computers

notable_claims: Library and computers are converging in function.
Offensiveness is not a legitimate reason to exclude material from a collection according to ALA standards.
Restricting access to materials via special accounts or signatures constitutes censorship.
classification.summary: Carl M. Kadie presents a framework for applying established library intellectual freedom and anti-censorship principles to the management of public and academic computer systems. He analyzes eight case studies involving newsgroup filtering, archive selection, and legal threats to demonstrate how library standards can prevent arbitrary censorship on the internet. The text argues that computers are converging with libraries and should adopt similar protections for privacy and free access.
classification.title: Applying library principles to computers

notable_claims: Banning newsgroups based on offensive content is a strong form of censorship and a violation of intellectual freedom principles.
Hate speech is generally protected by the Constitution as government cannot be trusted to define 'hateful'.
University restrictions on expression should only occur after competent legal advice and an adversarial hearing.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie argues against university censorship of Usenet newsgroups, specifically criticizing Penn State's removal of alt.sex groups. He asserts that banning content based on offensiveness violates academic freedom and that legal justifications regarding minors are often insufficient. The post provides a curated list of legal precedents regarding hate speech and expression to support the protection of digital communication.
